source: Dhami, Belton, Mandel et al. (2024) Matrix layout and confirmation bias in alternative hypotheses evaluation (Cognitive Research: Principles and Implications)
finding: Study 1 randomly assigned people to one of three layouts of the same evidence: hypotheses in columns with evidence in rows (the ACH-style matrix, HypCol), hypotheses in rows with evidence in columns (HypRow), or a text paragraph per hypothesis (HypText). Only HypRow reduced reliance on supporting evidence alone.
numbers: N=161 UK university staff and students (mean age 20.0, 90.1% female). HypCol n=55, HypRow n=51, HypText n=55. Each did 3 tasks, each with 2 hypotheses and 12 evidence items. Paper and pencil, no time limit, 10 pound voucher.
quote: individuals presented with hypotheses in rows and evidence items in columns were significantly less likely to demonstrate confirmation bias
limits: Not preregistered. Young, mostly female student sample, two hypotheses only, one decisive task (Task 1) classifies strategy. Authors say they cannot split BAL from INCONS in Study 1.
agent_relevance: The layout of the evidence changes which strategy is used. Our S4 presentation should be hypotheses as rows, evidence as columns, or at least tested against that.

source: Dhami, Belton, Mandel et al. (2024) Matrix layout and confirmation bias in alternative hypotheses evaluation (Cognitive Research: Principles and Implications)
finding: Strategy was read from the Task 1 choice. Choosing Hypothesis-A means the person leaned on consistent evidence only (CONS). Choosing Hypothesis-B means they balanced or used inconsistent evidence (BAL or INCONS). Overall 56.5% chose A (CONS) and 43.5% chose B.
numbers: Pooled over the three layouts, N=161. Self-reported strategy matched choice: chi2(2)=28.85, p<.001, phi=.49. 74.6% of A-choosers said they relied only on consistent evidence. A-choosers rated consistent evidence as more useful (M=5.64, SD=2.27) than inconsistent (M=5.05, SD=2.23), t(90)=2.43, d=0.26.
limits: Strategy is inferred from one forced choice; the design deliberately makes counts of consistent and inconsistent items point to different answers.
agent_relevance: Shows how to build a diagnostic probe: design items so that each reasoning strategy gives a different answer. We can use the same trick to test our agent.

source: Dhami, Belton, Mandel et al. (2024) Matrix layout and confirmation bias in alternative hypotheses evaluation (Cognitive Research: Principles and Implications)
finding: The layout effect on strategy was significant, and it is carried by the HypRow group alone. Most HypRow participants chose Hypothesis-B (balanced or inconsistent-evidence strategy). Most HypCol and HypText participants chose Hypothesis-A (supporting evidence only).
numbers: chi2(2)=9.43, p=.009, phi=.24. Bonferroni post hoc: HypRow differs from chance p=.003; HypCol p=.327; HypText p=.048 (borderline). Exact cell counts are in an image table (not extracted).
limits: Small to medium effect (phi .24). HypText p=.048 is borderline, so text is not clearly worse than matrix. Table 1 counts are not machine-readable here.
agent_relevance: The standard ACH matrix did no better than prose. Rotating the table is a free change, if the effect holds.

source: Dhami, Belton, Mandel et al. (2024) Matrix layout and confirmation bias in alternative hypotheses evaluation (Cognitive Research: Principles and Implications)
finding: The ACH-style matrix (hypotheses in columns) gave no advantage in sensitivity to evidence credibility. Credibility sensitivity was the same under all three layouts.
numbers: Among those who chose A on Task 3A (excluded 18%, 15%, 35% who chose B in HypCol, HypRow, HypText): 77% of HypCol, 78% of HypRow, 75% of HypText switched to B on Task 3B. chi2(2)=0.15, p=.927, phi=.04.
limits: Layout effect found for one bias facet only. The text condition had many more people who failed the pre-condition (35%).
agent_relevance: Layout may change what is attended to (consistency) without changing how well evidence quality is weighed. Credibility weighting needs a separate step or field in the schema.

source: Dhami, Belton, Mandel et al. (2024) Matrix layout and confirmation bias in alternative hypotheses evaluation (Cognitive Research: Principles and Implications)
finding: Cognitive reflection (CRT) was lower in people who used the supporting-evidence-only strategy in Study 1, but this did not replicate in analysts in Study 2.
numbers: Study 1: CONS group CRT M=0.27 (SD=0.68), BAL/INCONS M=0.81 (SD=1.00), t(116)=3.88, p<.001, Glass d=0.54. Study 2 analysts: 2.25 vs 2.34, t(60)=0.30, p=.763, d=0.10. Study 1 mean CRT 0.51 vs analysts 2.32, t(221)=13.68, d=2.05.
limits: Failed within-paper replication across populations. CRT floor effect in Study 1 (mean 0.51 of 3).
agent_relevance: Trait reflection is a weak predictor; a layout or a step in the scaffold is a more dependable lever than relying on 'careful' models.

source: Dhami, Belton, Mandel et al. (2024) Matrix layout and confirmation bias in alternative hypotheses evaluation (Cognitive Research: Principles and Implications)
finding: Study 2: Dutch military analysts (untrained in ACH) saw the ACH-style matrix and mostly did not show confirmation bias. Two thirds balanced supporting and opposing evidence.
numbers: N=62 analysts and officer cadets (80% male, mean age 32.5). Four tasks. CONS 19.4%, INCONS 14.5%, BAL 66.1%. Of those who chose A on Task 3A, 83.3% switched on 3B (credibility sensitive).
limits: Volunteers, anonymous, no control layouts in Study 2. Not preregistered. Classification rests on 2 forced-choice tasks.
agent_relevance: The 'humans are confirmation-biased' premise behind ACH is weaker than assumed. Do not assume the baseline model is biased; measure it.

source: Dhami, Belton, Mandel et al. (2024) Matrix layout and confirmation bias in alternative hypotheses evaluation (Cognitive Research: Principles and Implications)
finding: Among analysts, strategy predicted credibility sensitivity: balanced users were most sensitive, the strictly inconsistent-evidence (ACH-mandated) users least.
numbers: Sensitive to credibility: BAL 98%, CONS 72.7%, INCONS 33.3% (Study 2, N=62). Logistic regression: strategy a significant predictor.
limits: Small cell sizes (INCONS about 9 people). Correlational.
agent_relevance: Counting only inconsistent evidence (the ACH rule) can lose credibility weighting. Our scaffold should count both sides and weight by source quality.

source: Dhami, Belton, Mandel et al. (2024) Matrix layout and confirmation bias in alternative hypotheses evaluation (Cognitive Research: Principles and Implications)
finding: Judgmental coherence (probabilities summing to 1) did not separate good from poor performers in either study. Most people were nonadditive.
numbers: Study 2: 91.9% nonadditive, 24.2% superadditive, 67.7% subadditive; mean absolute deviation from additivity 15.42 (SD 12.23). CRT vs deviation: analysts r=-.12, p=.374.
limits: Nonadditivity was not related to strategy (t(60)=0.39, d=0.13 for Task 1).
agent_relevance: Coherence checks (summing to 1) are good hygiene but do not predict the right choice; do not rely on them as a quality signal.

source: Dhami, Belton, Mandel et al. (2024) Matrix layout and confirmation bias in alternative hypotheses evaluation (Cognitive Research: Principles and Implications)
finding: The authors give three possible reasons why hypotheses-in-rows layout helps: it supports sequential processing of one hypothesis at a time, it uses the horizontal dominance of human eye movement, and it matches left-to-right reading. These are proposals, not tested mechanisms.
numbers: No manipulation of the mechanism. Cited support: eye-movement and fluency studies (Deng 2016, Ojanpaa 2002, Gilchrist and Harvey 2006).
quote: a structure that facilitates sequential processing of information about each hypothesis may make the task less cognitively demanding
limits: Speculative, and the horizontal advantage is argued for left-to-right readers. Never tested here with eye tracking.
agent_relevance: For a text-only model the human-vision reasons do not apply. What may transfer is the order in which information is read: one hypothesis at a time.

source: Dhami, Belton, Mandel et al. (2024) Matrix layout and confirmation bias in alternative hypotheses evaluation (Cognitive Research: Principles and Implications)
finding: The paper summarises earlier ACH work: in a 50-analyst trial, 80% of the control group copied the textual data into an ACH-style matrix on their own; ACH-trained analysts had lower internal consistency and no better accuracy; law students (N=191) trained in ACH used the matrix only about a third of the time and rated its helpfulness 57 out of 100.
numbers: Dhami et al. 2019 / Mandel et al. 2018: 50 analysts, 4 hypotheses, 12 evidence items. Maegherman et al. 2020: N=191 law students.
limits: Secondary report of earlier studies, read inside the 2024 paper; originals not re-opened here.
agent_relevance: Making a matrix is a natural thing to do. Its benefit seems to come from what it exposes, not from the habit itself.

source: Dhami, Belton, Mandel et al. (2024) Matrix layout and confirmation bias in alternative hypotheses evaluation (Cognitive Research: Principles and Implications)
finding: Authors list limits and next steps: vary the number of hypotheses and evidence items, separate BAL from INCONS, test layouts in group work, check the CRT link in analyst samples. The horizontal advantage was never tested directly.
numbers: Tasks used two hypotheses and 12 evidence items throughout.
limits: Author-stated. I found no published replication of the Study 1 layout effect.
agent_relevance: Before depending on rows-over-columns, run our own small test with 2, 4 and 6 hypotheses.

source: Heuer (1999) Psychology of Intelligence Analysis, ch. 8 (CIA Center for the Study of Intelligence)
finding: Heuer sets the ACH layout: hypotheses across the top, evidence and arguments down the side. In Step 3 you work across the rows (one evidence item against all hypotheses). In Step 5 you work down the columns (one hypothesis against all evidence).
numbers: Eight steps in the ACH procedure. Matrix cells hold consistent / inconsistent / irrelevant notations, with credibility and relevance ratings for the evidence.
quote: prepare a matrix with hypotheses across the top and evidence down the side
limits: Heuer gave no experiment on the layout itself. The layout choice rests on his argument that a matrix puts the problem out of our head and onto paper.
agent_relevance: This is the claim Dhami 2024 tests: the layout that was recommended is the one that did not help.

source: Heuer (1999) Psychology of Intelligence Analysis, ch. 6 (car purchase matrix)
finding: Heuer's argument for the matrix as externalization: holding many options and attributes in working memory is hard, so put them on paper in a grid. He says to use it for important or controversial judgments, not every call, or when an audit trail is needed.
numbers: Worked example: car purchase with six attributes, matrix of alternatives by attributes; no empirical data.
quote: You may wish to do it, however, for an especially important, difficult, or controversial judgment
limits: Argument by example, not an experiment.
agent_relevance: Matches our S4 idea of presentation by code: put the grid in a structured block. The cost remark suggests we gate it by stakes.

source: Del Missier (2004) Properties of the decision environment and display organization in choice (ICCM-6)
finding: Reviews the cost-benefit theory of displays (Kleinmuntz and Schkade): a display is a cognitive incentive system that makes some strategies cheaper and others costlier, so it changes which strategy is chosen. Three display features matter: organization, form, and sequence. Two experiments plus a simulation compared a matrix with a Cartesian graph; no standard choice model fit all results; a variant of lexicographic choice (LEX-2) did.
numbers: Experiment 1: 60 undergraduates in four groups. Protocols: numeric encoding of values in 73% of compatible-graph statements vs 20% of incompatible-graph statements, p=.009. Simulation accuracy: LEX-2 about 71-73%, LEX about 35-38%.
limits: Choice among attribute-described options, not hypothesis evaluation. Small groups. A conference paper citing earlier work.
agent_relevance: Gives a formal frame: the layout alters the cost of strategies. Our S4 can be viewed as choosing which strategy is cheap for the model.

source: Kleinmuntz and Schkade (1993) Information displays and decision processes (Psychological Science 4, 221-227)
finding: Argues that displays shape decision processes by making some strategies easier and others harder (cost-benefit view). Known from a quotation in Del Missier (read) and a search snippet; the paper itself was not opened.
numbers: Not extracted.
limits: Not opened; only secondary description.
agent_relevance: Foundational frame for display effects on strategy; treat details as unverified.

source: Schkade and Kleinmuntz (1994) Information displays and choice processes: differential effects of organization, form, and sequence (OBHDP 57, 319-337)
finding: Search-snippet summary: organization (matrix vs list) had the strongest effect on information acquisition; form (numbers vs words) the strongest effect on combining and evaluating; sequence limited effect on acquisition. All three affected effort, organization most.
numbers: 60 MBA students chose among 8 loan applications on 4 attributes; processes inferred from protocols and times (from search result).
limits: Only a bibliographic summary was seen. Not opened. Attribute-choice task, not hypothesis testing.
agent_relevance: Best direct precedent that the organization of the grid changes acquisition order. Verify before quoting numbers.

source: Larkin and Simon (1987) Why a diagram is (sometimes) worth ten thousand words (Cognitive Science 11, 65-99)
finding: Classic model: two representations can hold the same information yet differ in computation, because grouping by location makes search and recognition cheaper. My fetch failed (HTTP 403); this is background knowledge only.
numbers: None extracted.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Basis for treating a layout as a computational choice, not decoration. Verify before quoting.

source: Sui, Zhou, Zhou, Han, Zhang (2024) Table Meets LLM: can LLMs understand structured table data? (WSDM 2024)
finding: Benchmark of table serialization choices for GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 on seven structural tasks. Input format changed accuracy sharply; HTML gave the best average. Self-augmented prompting added 0.84 to 5.68 points on five table QA sets.
numbers: GPT-3.5 average over 7 tasks: HTML highest at 65.43%. Size detection: HTML 67.00% vs 42.00% NL+sep, 40.67% Markdown, 42.67% JSON, 43.67% XML. Self-augmentation gains: TabFact +2.31, HybridQA +2.13, SQA +2.72, Feverous +0.84, ToTTo +5.68.
limits: Random subset of 300 samples per task for cost; flat relational tables only; GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 only; does not test rows-vs-columns for reasoning.
agent_relevance: How the table is written (HTML, markdown, JSON) changes what the model can perceive about structure. Use a format the model reads reliably and say what the layout means.

source: Sui et al. (2024) Table Meets LLM, ablations of helper text and examples
finding: Helper text matters in a task-dependent way: removing the format explanation or partition mark helped some tasks and hurt others. Removing the one-shot example hurt most.
numbers: GPT-3.5 HTML, removing the 1-shot example: drops of 12 to 50 points across tasks (largest -50.33). Removing format explanation: from +15 to -6.33 depending on the task.
limits: Task-by-task results are noisy on 300-sample subsets.
agent_relevance: An example of the layout beats a description of it. Show one filled matrix in the prompt.

source: Liu, Wang, Chen (2023) Rethinking tabular data understanding with large language models
finding: Same table content, different structure. Transposing a table (swapping rows and columns) cut GPT-3.5 accuracy; shuffling rows cut it less; both together cut it most. Code-based (symbolic) reasoning was far more fragile than text reasoning.
numbers: WikiTableQuestions, 837 questions, 4 variants (3,348 items). Direct prompting: original 59.50, row-shuffled 52.21 (-12.25%), transposed 51.14 (-14.05%), both 37.51 (-36.96%). Python agent: 55.91, 47.91 (-14.31%), 12.45 (-77.73%), 8.96 (-83.97%).
limits: GPT-3.5 only; one dataset; row labels in the extracted table were read from a text dump, but the percent drops are internally consistent.
agent_relevance: Row-per-record tables are the model's home layout. Hypotheses as rows (one record each) is likely the safer orientation for a text model too.

source: Liu, Wang, Chen (2023) Rethinking tabular data understanding with LLMs: transposition detection
finding: GPT-3.5 could not reliably detect a transposed layout. A normalizer (NORM) that detects and transposes column-tables to row-tables recovers accuracy.
numbers: GPT-3.5 labelled 93.35% of original tables as needing no transposition but only 32.54% of transposed tables correctly. Best mixed text+symbolic aggregation reached 73.6% on WikiTableQuestions.
limits: One model; structure bias only tested on a Wikipedia question set.
agent_relevance: The model does not notice when a grid is oriented oddly. So orient it in code and name the axes explicitly.

source: He et al. (2024) Does prompt formatting have any impact on LLM performance?
finding: The same content in plain text, Markdown, JSON or YAML changed GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 results a lot, and the best format differed by model and task. GPT-3.5 tended to like JSON, GPT-4 Markdown.
numbers: Up to 40% variation for GPT-3.5-turbo in code translation. On MMLU international law, accuracy up 42% for JSON vs Markdown (GPT-3.5-turbo-16k-0613). FIND: about 200% gain from Markdown to plain text. HumanEval with GPT-4-32k: over 300% from JSON to plain text. Only 16% identical responses between Markdown and JSON for GPT-3.5.
limits: Percent changes can be large from a small base. 2023-era GPT models. No hypothesis-matrix task.
agent_relevance: There is no universal best layout. Pick the S4 format by a quick test on our own model and re-test when the model changes.

source: Sclar, Choi, Tsvetkov, Suhr (2024) Quantifying language models' sensitivity to spurious features in prompt design (ICLR 2024)
finding: Meaning-preserving formatting changes (separators, spacing, casing) change few-shot accuracy by large amounts. The size of the change does not shrink with model size, number of examples or instruction tuning. Format performance correlates only weakly between models.
numbers: Up to 76 accuracy points of difference for LLaMA-2-13B between equivalent formats; about 20% of tasks show a large spread. Introduces FormatSpread to report a range.
limits: Open-source models of the time and few-shot classification-style tasks; no reasoning matrices.
agent_relevance: Report results over several layouts, not one. A scaffold gain on a single layout may be a format artefact.

source: Liu et al. (2024) Lost in the middle: how language models use long contexts
finding: Position of the relevant item inside the prompt matters: accuracy is highest at the start or end and falls in the middle (a U-shaped curve), even for long-context models.
numbers: GPT-3.5-Turbo multi-document QA can drop by more than 20% when the answer is in the middle; in the worst case it is below the 56.1% closed-book score. Key-value retrieval worst case 45.6% without query-aware contextualization; with it, 300 key-value pairs reached perfect accuracy for GPT-3.5-Turbo (16K).
limits: 2023 models; retrieval tasks. Newer models may have reduced the effect.
agent_relevance: Order of rows is a position effect. Put the question and the most decisive evidence at the start or end, and repeat the query after the grid.

source: Jhaveri, GX-Chen, Sucholutsky, Choi (2026) Failing to falsify: evaluating and mitigating confirmation bias in language models
finding: Eleven LLMs on a Wason-style rule-discovery task tend to propose confirming tests; more confirmation bias goes with lower success. Human-derived interventions (Dual-Goal, Think-in-Opposites) raise discovery.
numbers: Task success from 6% to 78% across models within 45 turns. Prompt intervention raised rule discovery from 42% to 56% on average. Reasoning-trace models show less bias. Distillation transfers to the Blicket test.
limits: Tests test selection, not evidence layout; synthetic number triples.
agent_relevance: Supports adding a falsification step, but says nothing about layout. LLM bias is real in exploration.

source: Lee, Kang, Shin (2026) Make LLMs see like investigators, not just think more: the role of structured analysis in investigative reasoning (PRISM, ACL 2026)
finding: A four-agent pipeline on the MuSR murder-mystery task builds an ACH evidence-by-suspect consistency matrix and counts inconsistencies, after a Motive/Means/Opportunity profiling step. The full pipeline beat plain prompting, CoT and self-consistency on all 10 models.
numbers: 10 LLMs (GPT-5.2, Qwen3, Llama, Mistral and others). Mean accuracy: Direct 58.1%, CoT 57.2%, Persona 58.2%, P-CoT 58.0%, Self-consistency (5 samples) 63.2%, PRISM 71.3% (+13.2 points; range +6.0 to +22.0). CoT lowered accuracy for some models.
limits: Fiction-based benchmark with a known answer; the ACH matrix is built by the model rather than shown to it; one benchmark.
agent_relevance: The only LLM test I found that includes an ACH matrix. It is a pipeline test, not a layout test.

source: Lee, Kang, Shin (2026) PRISM ablation of the ACH matrix step
finding: Almost all the gain came from information filtering and M.O.M.A profiling. Adding the ACH matrix on top added little (+0.8 points, 11% of the gain).
numbers: Filtering plus final judge only (P1P4): 63.8%. Adding M.O.M.A (P1P2P4): 70.5% (+6.7, 89% of the structured-analysis gain). Full with ACH: 71.3% (+0.8). Filtering alone beat Direct 58.1%, CoT 57.2% and Self-consistency 63.2%.
limits: Single benchmark; ACH not isolated from its prompts; no layout variants.
agent_relevance: Agrees with the human evidence that the ACH matrix is not where the value is. Spend effort on what goes in (filtering, profiling) rather than the grid.

source: Synthesis across opened sources: gap in layout evidence for LLM hypothesis evaluation
finding: Human layout effects exist (hypotheses as rows) but only for one bias facet, two hypotheses, and students. LLM table studies show layout and format matter for models but none test hypothesis evaluation. I found no study that runs rows vs columns vs prose for LLM hypothesis evaluation.
numbers: Human: N=161 and N=62. LLM: Sui, Liu, He, Sclar, Lost in the middle with table or retrieval tasks.
limits: The gap claim rests on a limited search (3 web searches, a few API queries; OpenAlex was rate-limited, arXiv search returned nothing).
agent_relevance: The open question is ours to test: run hypotheses-in-rows vs columns vs prose on our agent and measure the strategy choice at 2, 4 and 6 hypotheses.
